questions.answer: It is an event-type interrupt: the event is latched into INTR_STATE and stays set until cleared, by writing 1 to INTR_STATE0 or by writing COMPARE_LOWER0_0/COMPARE_UPPER0_0. The comparison is an unsigned 64-bit mtime >= mtimecmp.
Counting is gated by CTRL.active_0. The timer operates only when it is 1, and software is expected to configure the registers before activating the timer.

Verify the fixed configuration of one hart and one timer (N_HARTS=1, N_TIMERS=1). The multi-timer and multi-hart text, including the per-hart enable/state sets, describes a configurable example (N_TIMER 2, N_HARTS 2). It does not apply to this version.

The documents say a tick occurs when the internal counter hits CFG0.prescaler. They do not say whether the counter is reset to 0 afterwards. They do not define the behaviour for prescaler = 0. They do not define what happens if prescaler or step change while running; they only say the fields must be stable.
The interrupt is latched event-type (see Q0). The documents do not say whether the compare is evaluated every clock cycle or only on ticks. The designer must decide this.

The documents say writing either compare register can clear the interrupt source. They do not say whether the clear is unconditional or whether the interrupt re-asserts when mtime >= the new mtimecmp still holds. The designer must decide.
The stability requirement is stated as a software obligation. The documents do not say whether hardware ignores or tolerates changes while active, or what the DUT does if they change.
With a step above 1, mtime can skip over mtimecmp at wraparound, and the interrupt is not raised. This is documented behaviour.
The register-level reset default is 0x0 and the wo field reset is x. The documents do not say what a read of a write-only register or field returns after reset. The designer must specify that.
The documents do not say what reads of ALERT_TEST bit 0 (wo) return. They do not say why the reset mask includes bit 0. The designer must decide.
Writing 0 to regwen disables alert testing, meaning ALERT_TEST writes no longer trigger fatal_fault test alerts, until the next reset. It says nothing about blocking genuine bus-integrity alerts.
The documents do not state that reserved bits read as 0 or that writes to them are ignored. They only mark the bits Reserved. The designer must decide.
Not needed for verification: RACL is disabled in the verification top, so every register access is permitted and no access is rejected for an access-control reason.

It is stated as a configuration fact of the integration top, in INT-CFG-003 alongside the synchronous alert clocking scheme. It covers the only alert channel, fatal_fault. The documents do not say why pings are never issued.
Yes. Reset values come from the rv_timer register tables, and every register holds its reset value while rst_ni is 0. Verification of reset values of every register is observed through the ports.

The documents say only that outputs change at the rising clock edge 'except for the effect of rst_ni', and that reset asserts asynchronously. They do not say whether the exemption covers every cycle with rst_ni low or only the assertion edge. The designer must decide.
Legal opcodes are Get=4, PutFullData=0 and PutPartialData=1. All others are undefined, and devices should return an error, with d_error=1 for unsupported opcodes.

o_alert is 1 for one clock cycle for each alert handshake the receiver detects. o_d_intg_err is evaluated per cycle: it is 1 in a cycle where o_d_valid is 1 and the response integrity check fails, and 0 otherwise.

The documents do not define the latency of the fatal_fault alert after a command integrity error, and say they do not specify the D-channel response to such a request. Alert latency is therefore undefined and must be set by the designer.

The documents say one alert event yields one alert handshake and o_alert is 1 for one cycle per handshake. They give no expected latency through the sender/receiver handshake and do not guarantee exactly one pulse. The designer must decide.

The documents say only that a fatal alert repeats until reset. In the alert handler spec the sender waits 2 cycles between handshakes, but the handshake length in the synchronous scheme is not given. No repeat interval or bound is defined.

Verify that the event latches into INTR_STATE, the output is INTR_STATE AND INTR_ENABLE, writing 1 to INTR_TEST sets INTR_STATE, and writing 1 to INTR_STATE clears it. If the event is still active after the clear, the state returns to 1. Hardware cannot clear the state.

The documents do not say whether natural counting must also be exercised. They require coverage of counting including the lower-to-upper carry, and say near-2^64 behaviour is reached by writing the timer value registers. Whether natural counting is required is a designer decision.
The documents say a baseline source generates a project-specific default value. They do not give the value or say whether it is constant, so it cannot be checked.
No bursts means transaction sizes are limited to the bus width (byte, 2B, 4B). The checkable condition on this 32-bit bus is a_size <= 2, and a larger a_size is an error.
For this project's 32-bit bus (DW=32, SZW 2 bits for 4B), a_size greater than 2 is an error. The 'h3 size for PutFullData applies only if a 64b bus width is supported, so there is no conflict here.

The TL-UL spec says non-contiguous masks are device-dependent: devices may or may not support them and may assert d_error. The register tool says writes smaller than the register size return an error. How rv_timer treats a non-contiguous mask on a full-word access is not stated.

The documents say INTR_STATE is ro for Status type and that the interrupt is formed directly from the input signal. They do not say whether INTR_STATE mirrors the input or whether INTR_TEST applies to Status type. rv_timer uses Event type, so this is outside its scope.

INTR_TEST is a write-only register that asserts the interrupt for testing. Writing 1 to the INTR_TEST bit sets the corresponding INTR_STATE bit, so the function is defined by both quotes, and 'can' does not make it optional.
Software cannot clear fatal cause registers in any way; they are read-only. Reset is the exception: fatal alerts persist until reset, and rst_ni puts the whole IP into a defined state.
No. A cause register is only recommended for IPs with multiple bundled alerts. The must-rules on clearability apply to cause registers that exist.

The register tool says unmapped addresses 'typically' return an error and that excess address bits are stripped, so aliased addresses may not error. rv_timer's internal address width is not given, so which unmapped addresses must error cannot be determined. The designer must decide.

The documents say software has precedence, and if the event is still true the clear lasts one cycle and q returns to 1. The exact resulting value for bit-level collisions depends on a logic figure that is not quoted. The designer must specify it.
It is only recommended and may be relaxed, not mandatory. Error handling on a window's bus is under the control of the logic managing it.
The documents say the sender waits 2 cycles between handshakes (2 sender cycles). They do not say from which edge this is measured or whether 2 is exact or a minimum.
Yes. Pingfail is raised after a programmable ping timeout, set via PING_TIMEOUT_CYC_SHADOWED, so latency is bounded by that configured timeout.
